lessons.t: The agent loop: model, tools, environment, stopping condition
lessons.html:
An agent is a model calling tools in a loop. Each turn, the model reads its context, chooses an action, the harness executes it against some environment, and the result goes back into context. The loop ends when a stopping condition fires. Every agent you will ever spec has these four parts, and most agent failures can be traced to one of them.

PartWhat it isThe PM question
ModelChooses the next action from what it can seeIs this model good at choosing actions on our tasks, measured over whole runs?
ToolsThe actions available: search, read, write, run code, call an APICan the task be finished with these tools, and nothing more dangerous?
EnvironmentThe system the tools act on, and the feedback it returnsDoes the environment tell the agent clearly when it is wrong?
Stopping conditionWhat ends the loop: success, failure, budget or a personWho decides “done”, and what happens at the limit?

Workflow or agent

Anthropic’s guidance draws a useful line. In a workflow, your code fixes the sequence of model calls and tools. In an agent, the model decides the sequence. Workflows are cheaper, faster and easier to test. Agents earn their cost when the number of steps can’t be known in advance: debugging, research, triage across many systems. Many features that get pitched as agents are better as a two-step workflow or a single well-built call.

A practical test for act versus answer: if a competent person could finish the task by reading and writing a reply, answer. If they would need to look things up, try something, check the result and adjust, an agent may pay off. If they would follow the same five steps every time, write a workflow.

Why the environment matters most

Coding agents matured first because code has a strong feedback signal. Tests pass or fail, the compiler complains, the linter points to the line. Agents improve sharply when the environment returns precise, checkable feedback, and drift when it returns vague success messages. Before you ask “which model?”, ask what signal the agent gets after each action. A CRM API that returns 200 OK for a malformed update gives the agent nothing to correct against.

Stopping conditions

Write at least four into the spec:

  • Success. Ideally confirmed by a verifier (tests pass, record matches schema, reviewer approves) as well as by the model’s own judgement.
  • Step and spend caps. A hard limit on turns, tokens and wall-clock time. Loops that repeat the same failing call are a common and expensive failure.
  • Give-up rule. When the agent should stop and report what it tried, rather than keep going.
  • Interrupt. A person can halt the run at any point, and the agent leaves the system in a known state.

Common failure

Agents more often stop too early than run forever. They declare success after a partial fix, or answer from memory instead of using the search tool. Premature stopping is invisible unless your eval checks the end state of the environment, not the agent’s final message.

What changes for you

  • Before approving an agent, ask whether a fixed workflow would do. Ask the team to argue for the loop.
  • Specify the four stopping conditions explicitly, with numbers for the caps.
  • Grade agent evals on the end state of the environment (Chapter 5). The agent’s own summary of what it did is weak evidence.

lessons.t: Designing tools models can use well
lessons.html:
The model only knows a tool through its name, description, parameter schema and what it returns. That is an interface, and a model is a demanding user of it: it reads every word, takes names literally and can’t ask a colleague what a field means. Anthropic calls this the agent-computer interface and recommends spending as much effort on it as on a human UI. In practice, tool design moves agent quality as much as model choice does.

Wrap the user’s task

The most common mistake is exposing your REST API one endpoint at a time. Suppose a support agent needs a customer’s recent failed orders. With list_customers, get_customer, list_orders and get_order, the agent makes four or more calls, pages through irrelevant records and fills its context with JSON. A single find_customer_orders(customer_email, status, since) returning order number, date, status and failure reason does the same job in one call. Fewer calls means fewer chances to go wrong (see lesson 5) and less context consumed.

Anti-patternWhat the agent doesFix
One tool per endpointChains many calls, loses trackConsolidate around the task the user actually has
Opaque IDs in responsesPasses the wrong ID or invents oneReturn readable names alongside IDs; offer a concise and a detailed format
Unbounded responsesFloods context with thousands of rowsPaginate, filter and truncate by default, and say so in the response
Error codes and stack tracesRetries the same bad callErrors that say what was wrong and show a valid example
Overlapping toolsPicks the wrong one at randomOne clear owner per job; namespace by service, such as billing_search
Vague parameter namesGuesses the formatuser_email instead of user; state units and formats

Make mistakes hard

Anthropic’s SWE-bench work found that requiring absolute file paths removed a whole class of errors. The same idea applies everywhere: enums instead of free text, required fields instead of optional ones, a dry_run flag on anything that writes, and idempotency keys so a retried call doesn’t create a second refund. Separate read tools from write tools. That split is what lets you approve writes without approving every lookup (lesson 6).

Tool definitions cost tokens

Every tool’s definition is sent on every call. Dozens of tools with long descriptions can take thousands of tokens before the user has said anything, and too many similar tools measurably confuse selection. Keep the default set small, load specialised tools only when needed (skills and tool search do this), and keep definitions stable and in a fixed order so prompt caching works (Chapter 4).

Test tools the way you test UI

Run the agent on 20 realistic tasks and read the transcripts. Look for calls with wrong arguments, repeated calls, and responses the agent ignored. Each pattern points to a specific fix in a name, description, default or error message. Agents can help here: give one the transcripts and ask it to propose tool changes, then re-run the eval.

What changes for you

  • Review tool names, descriptions and error messages as product copy. They are the agent’s UI.
  • Ask for a tool inventory in every agent spec: which tools, read or write, what they return, how big the response can be.
  • Require a dry-run and an idempotency key on every write tool before it goes near production.

lessons.t: MCP, A2A and skills: the emerging standard stack
lessons.html:
Three open standards now cover most of how agents connect to the rest of the world. They solve different problems, and a serious deployment usually uses all three. Status below is as of October 2026.

StandardWhat it standardisesUnitGovernance
MCP (Model Context Protocol)How an agent connects to tools and dataAn MCP server exposing tools, resources and promptsAgentic AI Foundation (Linux Foundation), founding project
A2A (Agent2Agent)How agents discover each other and delegate tasks across vendorsAn agent with a published Agent CardLinux Foundation since June 2025; accepted into the Agentic AI Foundation in August 2026
Agent SkillsHow procedural knowledge is packaged and loaded on demandA folder with a SKILL.md plus optional scripts and referencesOpen specification at agentskills.io, originally from Anthropic

MCP

Anthropic released MCP in late 2024. On 9 December 2025 the Linux Foundation launched the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) with three founding projects: MCP from Anthropic, goose from Block and AGENTS.md from OpenAI. Its platinum members include AWS, Anthropic, Block, Bloomberg, Cloudflare, Google, Microsoft and OpenAI. MCP is supported by the main agent clients, IDEs and coding agents, so an MCP server you build once is usable from most of them.

The current specification revision is 2026-07-28, and it changed a lot. The protocol is now stateless: the initialise handshake and protocol-level sessions are gone, and each request carries its own version and capabilities. Servers must implement server/discover. Long-running work moved into an official tasks extension with polling. Sampling, roots and logging are deprecated. Servers should return tools in a deterministic order to help prompt caching. For you, stateless servers are easier to run behind ordinary load balancers, which lowers the cost of hosting your own.

A2A

Google introduced A2A in April 2025 and the Linux Foundation took it on in June 2025. Version 1.0 was the first stable specification, and by April 2026 the Linux Foundation reported more than 150 supporting organisations and integrations in Azure AI Foundry, Copilot Studio and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. In August 2026 A2A was accepted into AAIF as a growth-stage project, so the tool layer and the agent layer now sit in one foundation. An A2A agent publishes an Agent Card describing what it can do and how to authenticate, and other agents send it tasks that can run long and stream updates.

Use A2A when the other side is an agent you don’t control, such as a supplier’s or a SaaS vendor’s, and you want to hand over a goal rather than call a function. If you control both sides, an MCP tool or a subagent is usually simpler.

Skills

A skill is a folder with a SKILL.md file (name, description, instructions) and optional scripts, references and templates. Agents load only the name and description at startup, read the full instructions when a task matches, and open bundled files only when needed. This progressive disclosure (Chapter 4) lets an agent carry hundreds of skills at little context cost. The format is published as an open standard, and the agentskills.io client list includes Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot, Cursor and VS Code.

Trust boundary

An MCP server or a skill is code and instructions running with your agent’s permissions. A malicious or careless one can read data it shouldn’t, or carry injected instructions. Treat installing one like adding a dependency with production access (Chapter 12).

What changes for you

  • Put a standards line in agent specs: which MCP servers, which skills, any A2A peers, and who owns each.
  • Prefer building an MCP server over a bespoke integration. It works across clients and survives a model or vendor switch.
  • Package your team’s repeatable procedures (release notes, QA checklists, data pulls) as skills, versioned in git.
  • Re-check this lesson each quarter. The specs are moving and dated facts here will age.

Computer use lets a model operate a graphical interface: it receives screenshots and returns mouse and keyboard actions. Browser agents do the same inside a web browser, often with access to the page structure as well as pixels. They reach software that has no API, which in most enterprises is a lot of software: legacy admin consoles, supplier portals, government forms, internal tools nobody will ever wrap.

The interface hierarchy

Choose the highest rung available for each step. Each step down is slower, costlier and more fragile.

InterfaceSpeed and costReliabilityUse when
Direct API or MCP toolFast, cheapHighestAn API exists or can be built
Browser via page structure (DOM, accessibility tree)ModerateGood on stable pagesWeb app with no API
Pixels and coordinatesSlow; every step sends a screenshotLowest; breaks on layout changes, pop-ups, resolutionDesktop apps, canvases, last resort

A task that takes one API call can take 30 screen actions, each a model turn with an image in context. Expect minutes per task, and cost per task one to two orders of magnitude above an API route (illustrative; measure yours). That still beats a person doing it by hand for many back-office jobs, which is where computer use earns its keep: high-volume, tedious, low-judgement tasks on stable screens.

The security problem is the product problem

A browser agent reads untrusted content all day. Any page, email or document it opens can contain instructions aimed at the model. In August 2025 Anthropic published red-team results for its Chrome extension pilot: across 123 test cases, prompt-injection attacks succeeded 23.6% of the time without mitigations and 11.2% with them in autonomous mode. Mitigations have improved since, but no vendor claims zero. An agent that is logged into your email, your bank and your CRM while reading arbitrary web pages has all three parts of the lethal trifecta (Chapter 12).

Design controls that work

  • Separate identity. A dedicated browser profile or VM, logged into only what the task needs.
  • Site allowlists. The agent may visit the supplier portal and nothing else.
  • Confirmation on consequential actions. Publishing, purchasing, sending and sharing personal data pause for a person, even in autonomous mode.
  • Session recording. Store the screenshots and actions so a failed run can be replayed and audited.
  • Graduate to an API. Once a computer-use flow proves valuable, that is the evidence you need to build or buy the API.

Where it breaks

CAPTCHAs and bot detection, multi-factor prompts, session timeouts, unexpected modals and A/B tests on the target site. Budget for a human handoff path from day one, and track the share of runs that need it.

What changes for you

  • In specs, state which interface rung each step uses and why a higher rung isn’t available.
  • Never ship a browser agent with access to accounts it doesn’t need for the task. Scope the identity first.
  • Track cost and time per completed task against the manual baseline. That number decides whether the feature lives.

lessons.t: Compounding error: why 95% per step is 36% over 20 steps
lessons.html:
If each step of a task succeeds independently with probability p, a task of n steps succeeds with probability pn. The numbers are brutal.

Per-step success5 steps10 steps20 steps50 steps
95%77%60%36%8%
99%95%90%82%61%
99.5%98%95%90%78%
99.9%99.5%99%98%95%

To hit 90% task success over 20 steps you need about 99.5% per step. A model that looks excellent on single answers can be unusable on long chains. This is why demos of agents mislead: a demo is one successful sample of a long chain.

Where the simple model is wrong

Real agents are better and worse than the formula:

  • Better, because errors can be recovered. A failing test, a clear error message or a re-read of the file lets the agent notice and fix a mistake. What compounds is the unrecovered error rate. Good environments and good error messages (lesson 2) shrink it.
  • Worse, because errors correlate. One wrong assumption early, such as editing the wrong customer record, poisons every later step. The agent then works hard and competently on the wrong problem.
  • Worse, because context degrades. Long runs fill the context with tool output, and quality falls as it grows (Chapter 4). Step 40 is often less reliable than step 4.

Task length is the capability to watch

METR measures a model’s time horizon: the length of task, in human expert time, that it completes with a given probability. In its March 2025 study the 50% horizon had doubled roughly every seven months over six years. Two product lessons follow. The tasks agents can do will keep getting longer, so revisit your scoping every quarter (Chapter 3). And a 50% horizon is a capability number. Your product needs the much shorter horizon at which success is 90% or higher, the pass^k view from Chapter 1.

Levers, in order of cost

  1. Fewer steps. Consolidated tools and workflows for the predictable parts.
  2. Verifiers. Checks after key steps (tests, schema validation, a second model checking a diff) that catch errors before they compound.
  3. Checkpoints. Save state at milestones so a failure resumes from step 12.
  4. Safe retries. Idempotent write tools so a retry is harmless.
  5. Human approval at irreversible steps, which resets the error chain at the point where errors are most costly.

Failure budget

For each agent, state the acceptable rate of failed runs, of runs needing human rescue and of runs causing harm, separately. An illustrative budget for an internal ops agent: ≤ 15% of runs hand off to a person, ≤ 2% finish with a wrong result that a person later catches, 0 irreversible wrong actions. Track all three weekly.

What changes for you

  • Ask for per-step and per-run success separately. If only per-run is reported, ask how many steps a typical run takes.
  • Cut steps before you buy a bigger model. Each removed step raises the ceiling for every run.
  • Put a failure budget in every agent spec, with a separate line for irreversible harm.

lessons.t: Autonomy levels, approvals and long-running background agents
lessons.html:
Chapter 1 named four autonomy levels: suggest, draft, act with approval, act. Choosing among them is the most consequential decision in an agent spec, and the right level is set per action. A single agent might read freely, draft emails for review and require approval to issue refunds.

Choosing a level per action

Action is…Reversible and cheap if wrongReversible but costlyIrreversible or external
Output is easy to verifyActAct, with audit log and alertsAct with approval
Output is hard to verifyAct with spot checksAct with approvalDraft or suggest only

Moving up a level should be earned with evidence: an eval on real tasks, then a period at the lower level where you measure how often people change or reject the agent’s proposal. If reviewers approve 98% of refund proposals unchanged over 500 cases, that is a case for auto-approving small refunds. If they edit 30%, the agent isn’t ready, whatever the offline eval says.

Designing approvals people actually read

Approval fatigue is real. A person asked to confirm forty routine actions an hour stops reading and clicks yes, and the approval becomes theatre. Better patterns:

  • Approve the plan once. The agent proposes “update 14 records, email 3 customers, close ticket”, a person approves once, and the agent executes within that plan.
  • Risk-tier the gates. Gate by amount, audience or data sensitivity. Refunds under an illustrative $50 auto-approve; above that, a person decides.
  • Show the diff. Present what will change, in the system’s own terms, with the agent’s evidence attached.
  • Make rejection useful. A rejection with a reason should go into the trace and the eval set.

Background agents

Agents increasingly run for many minutes or hours with nobody watching. Coding agents such as Claude Code, OpenAI Codex and GitHub Copilot’s coding agent take a task, work in a cloud sandbox and return a pull request. The pull request is the approval surface, and the pattern generalises: the agent works in isolation and hands back an artefact a person can review, accept or discard. Protocols are catching up, with long-running task support in both MCP’s tasks extension and A2A.

RequirementWhy it matters for long runs
Isolated sandboxMistakes stay contained; nothing touches production until reviewed
Hard budgetsTime, tokens and spend caps per run, with an alert before the cap
Checkpoints and resumeA crash or timeout at hour two doesn’t restart from zero
Full traceEvery tool call and result stored, so a reviewer can see how it got there (Chapter 10)
Kill switchStop one run or all runs, leaving systems in a known state
Notification designTell people when review is needed and when it isn’t, or they stop looking

The real bottleneck

Background agents shift work from doing to reviewing. Ten agents producing ten pull requests a day is only progress if someone can review ten pull requests a day. Plan reviewer capacity as part of the launch (Chapter 8).

What changes for you

  • Specify autonomy per action in a table, with the evidence needed to move each action up a level.
  • Measure approval rates and edit rates at the gated level. They are your promotion criteria.
  • For background agents, spec the review artefact (diff, report, pull request) as carefully as the agent itself.
  • Budget reviewer time. Agent throughput beyond review capacity only builds a queue.

lab.title: Build and trace a three-tool MCP agent
lab.intro: You will build a small agent for a real workflow, run it ten times and read every step. The point is to see where long chains break and to turn that into an autonomy level and a failure budget you can defend.
steps: Pick the workflow. Choose a real task from your team that takes a person 10–30 minutes and 5–15 steps, touches at least two systems and ends in one write action. Examples: triage a bug report into a ticket, prepare a weekly account summary, reconcile a supplier invoice.

Write ten task cases. Use real past instances. For each, record the correct end state of the system (the ticket fields, the summary facts) so you can grade the result itself. Include two hard cases and one that should end in “I can’t do this”.

Expose three MCP tools. Two read tools and one write tool. Use existing MCP servers where they exist, or write thin ones. Apply lesson 2: consolidated, readable responses, bounded output, actionable errors, and a dry_run flag on the write tool. Point the write tool at a sandbox or test account.

Run in a client that traces. Use any MCP-capable agent client or SDK that records every tool call, argument, result, token count and timing. Set caps: 30 steps, 15 minutes and a token budget per run. Keep the write tool in dry-run for the first pass.

Run the ten cases and read every trace. In the template, log each run’s steps, end-state correctness, cost and time. Mark the first step where the run went wrong and classify it: wrong tool, bad arguments, misread result, premature stop, loop, or unsafe action.
Fix and re-run. Make at most three changes, preferably to tool names, descriptions, defaults or errors, and re-run all ten cases. Record what moved.
Set the autonomy level and failure budget. For each tool action, choose suggest, draft, act with approval or act using lesson 6’s matrix, and write a failure budget from what you observed.

RunStepsEnd state correct?First wrong stepFailure typeTokensTimeNotes
1Yes / Partly / No

10
TotalsMedian:Pass rate:Most common:Median:p90:Implied per-step success:
lab.done: You have ten readable traces, a failure-type count, a before-and-after comparison from your fixes, and a per-action autonomy table backed by evidence. You can say which failure type dominates and whether a tool change or a model change is the cheaper fix. Keep the agent: Chapter 12’s lab attacks it.

quiz.q: A team proposes an agent to generate a weekly report. It always pulls the same three dashboards, computes the same deltas and writes a summary. What should you push for?
o: A more capable model so the agent rarely fails
A fixed workflow with one or two model calls, since the steps are known in advance
Computer use, so the agent can read the dashboards visually
An A2A integration with the dashboard vendor’s agent
quiz.w: When the sequence of steps is predictable, a workflow is cheaper, faster and easier to test. Agents pay off when the steps can’t be known in advance.

quiz.q: Your support agent keeps calling list_orders repeatedly and running out of steps. Its traces show it paging through hundreds of irrelevant orders. What is the best first fix?
o: Raise the step cap from 30 to 100
Switch to a reasoning model with a larger context window
Add a consolidated, filtered tool that returns only the orders relevant to the customer’s question
Add few-shot examples of paging correctly
quiz.w: The tool shape forces many calls and floods context. Consolidating around the task removes steps, which also improves reliability under compounding error.

quiz.q: A partner company offers an agent that handles freight booking end to end. You want your procurement agent to hand it shipments and receive status updates over several days. Which standard fits?
o: A2A, because you’re delegating a long-running task to an agent you don’t control
MCP sampling, so the partner can call your model
A skill, packaged with the partner’s instructions
Computer use against the partner’s booking website
quiz.w: A2A is for discovering and delegating tasks to other agents across organisations, including long-running work. MCP connects an agent to tools you call; sampling is now deprecated in MCP.

quiz.q: An agent has 98% per-step success and typical runs of 30 steps. Engineering says it’s “98% reliable”. What run-level success should you expect if errors aren’t recovered?
o: About 98%
About 74%
About 55%
About 30%
quiz.w: 0.98³⁰ ≈ 0.55. Per-step and per-run reliability differ sharply on long chains, so ask for both.

quiz.q: Reviewers of an agent’s refund proposals now approve almost everything within two seconds. Approval rates are 99%. What does this most likely mean?
o: The agent is ready to act fully autonomously on all refunds
Approval fatigue: the gate has become a rubber stamp, so redesign it around risk tiers and plan-level approval
Reviewers need more training on the refund policy
The eval set is too small
quiz.w: Instant approvals suggest people have stopped reading. Gate high-risk actions meaningfully and auto-approve low-risk ones with audit, rather than asking for clicks on everything.

quiz.q: A browser agent will book travel using employees’ logged-in browsers and read arbitrary airline and hotel pages. What is the most important design change?
o: Use the pixel interface instead of the DOM for robustness
Increase the step cap so bookings finish
Add a skill describing each airline’s booking flow
Run in a separate profile with only the booking account, a site allowlist, and confirmation before any purchase
quiz.w: Browser agents read untrusted content that can carry injected instructions. Scoping identity and sites and confirming consequential actions limits what an injection can do.

deliverable.title: Agent design doc
deliverable.html:
A one-page design doc for one agent feature. Engineering builds from it, security reviews it, and it states plainly what the agent may do on its own.

  1. Job and why an agent. The task in one sentence, who it’s for, and why a fixed workflow or single call won’t do.
  2. Loop. Model and thinking budget, environment, and the four stopping conditions with numbers: success check, step and spend caps, give-up rule, interrupt.
  3. Tool inventory. Each tool: name, read or write, standard (MCP server, skill, A2A peer, browser), owner, maximum response size, dry-run and idempotency for writes.
  4. Autonomy table. Each action: level (suggest, draft, act with approval, act), approval surface, and the evidence needed to move it up a level.
  5. Failure budget. Acceptable rates for failed runs, human rescue and wrong results caught later, plus zero tolerance items. Typical steps per run and measured per-step success.
  6. Evals and traces. The task set graded on end state (Chapter 5), trace storage and who reads traces weekly.
  7. Risks. Untrusted inputs the agent reads, data it can reach, ways out, and controls (Chapter 12).
  8. Long runs. Sandbox, checkpoints, kill switch, notification plan and reviewer capacity.

Review it again whenever the model, a tool or the autonomy level changes.
